en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of India during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in a vihāra in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. At dawn, he...
Having dressed in his morning robes, he called out to Ānanda:
"Invite the various wise ones, the assembly that has eliminated evil, Aśoka, Pāda-vikrama, and the others to come; today there shall be a supreme inquiry concerning extraordinary essentials."
Thereupon Ānanda received the command and immediately proclaimed the Tathāgata’s teaching throughout the fourfold assembly.

At that time, five hundred million people—including those who had eliminated evil, those who were free from attachment, and those who followed the tracks [of the path]—approached the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and having finished their salutations, withdrew to stand aside.

Furthermore, there were fourteen thousand virtuous women—including the woman who had abandoned evil, the common women of the kingdom, and those who followed the various virtuous women—who approached the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves on the ground, withdrew, and sat down.
Furthermore, there were eight hundred and twenty million two thousand wise men who went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves on the ground, and stood solemnly and respectfully.
Additionally, forty thousand scholars and householders who practiced the precepts followed one another to that place; they prostrated themselves on the ground and then each withdrew to stand aside.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he moved the wise ones and the supreme devas of the Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions—those who were ready for realization and those who were about to set forth in the path; eight hundred million people in all flew to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and stood in formation suspended in mid-air.

Furthermore, there were twelve celestial deities and generals who, leading their respective retinues of four hundred thousand beings, came to where the Buddha was. Having prostrated themselves upon the ground, they each took their positions and stood in attendance to the left and right of the Buddha.
On that very day, at the appointed time, they all arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling within the duration of a single meal; the Buddha then bade them sit.
Those with physical bodies who had not yet attained the four bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) were to take their places upon couches.

The wise men and celestial deities from the ten directions who had light bodies, or those who had already attained the bases of supernatural power, all leaped into the air and sat upon seats that appeared spontaneously. Each had a transformed flower-canopy, arranged in marvelous rows, all produced through the miraculous transformations of the Buddha’s majestic power.

All the wise men who have come and are seated in this assembly are for the most part practitioners of sublime conduct, with pure minds and clean speech, their bodies clad in the various precepts. The three impurities, the six afflictions, and the five obscurations have already been sought out and eliminated; the many fevers of vexation, the various defilements, the knots of the net of doubt, the errors of inverted views, the root of ignorance, and the twelve links of dependent origination have all been severed and cast away.
Pure as the moon and lotus, each followed worldly customs and established their names based on their conduct:
there was a wise man named King Without Defilement; next, he was named Honored One of Radiant Splendor; next, he was named Vast as a Mountain of Wisdom;
next, he was named Pure Great Flower; next, he was named Fragrance of Turning Roots; and next, he was named...
The Moon-Essence Radiance; next, again named Light-Supreme; next, again named Rectifying the Unlawful;
next, again named Goodness Among the Good; next, again named Kunlun Radiance; next, again named Sunlight Essence; next, again named Lion’s Majesty;
next, again named Mind of Miscellaneous Jewels; next, again named Blazing Wonder.
Next, he was named Virtue Universally Pervading; next, he was named Universally Harmonious and Agile; next, he was named Reverent in Upright Conduct;
next, he was named Office of Compassionate Benevolence; next, he was named Wisdom-Maker; next, he was named Dispeller of Knots;
next, he was named Fully Endowed with Dignified Manner; next, he was named Lofty and Remote Practice; and next, he was named Radiant Virtue.
The King was next named Lokapāla (Protector of the World), next named Lokanāyaka (Guide of the World), next named Mahābala (Great Power), next named Śuddha (Pure),
next named Devaguru (Teacher of the Gods), next named Sudarśana (Good Vision), and next named Avalokita (Observant);
such were his various names, each distinct from the others.

At that time, there was a son of noble lineage named Shanming (Good Wisdom), who came to the place where the Buddha was with five hundred companions, each of whom had an attendant carrying a parasol following him. He prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, then stood up and observed the assembly; it was magnificent on all four sides. Looking up into the air, he saw that they were all superior beings. The World-Honored One sat upon his seat, upright and dignified. He gave rise to a thought, saying: "Today is a day of great merit;
having encountered this assembly, I wish to provide food and drink to sustain them for one day."
"I have calculated all that I possess and find it insufficient to provide for them; if my offerings are not equal or appropriate, then this is no true giving.
What shall I do? Thereupon, the Buddha, knowing the thoughts in Shanming’s mind, comforted him, saying:
"Welcome, young man!"
"Have you ever heard the teaching that encourages one to follow the Dharma?
He replied, "I have not yet understood it; when it is time to rise, I simply rise—can this not be called wisdom?"
Regardless of whether it is little or much, if there is an expectation of something in return, it may be called giving.
As for what I was thinking just now: since the Tathāgata is here, why worry about not being able to accomplish it?

The Tathāgata is able to bring to completion what is unaccomplished and to fulfill what is insufficient, so that all are eternally sufficient and all tasks are eternally accomplished; this is called the Tathāgata.

As for the Tathāgata’s accomplishment, he does not rely on clothing, food, or objects of sensual pleasure, but rather relies upon the complete precepts. He does not listen to the delusions of the six afflictions or the five obscurations; he does not dwell on domestic pleasures, nor does he harbor thoughts of the four kinds of nutriment, nor does he possess the adornments of clothing, appearance, crowns, or turbans.
Amidst the notion of permanence, one knows the truth of impermanence;
dwelling in a realm of deluded pleasure, one awakens to its inevitable counterpart, suffering.
Within the chamber of craving for existence, one illuminates the fundamental nature of emptiness and non-existence.
Regarding the substance of the existence of sensation, it is clarified that the true nature is not the body.
Being without self, without action, without conditions, and without attachment—this is the realization of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching, Shanming felt joy in his heart, his fetters were untied, and his body leaped with lightness.

He said: "I was originally without wisdom, bound by the twelve links; my mind arose toward darkness and I fell into the three worldly currents. What I have heard today is a Dharma never before encountered. I vow to receive and uphold it in person, following the World-Honored One’s instruction, and shall delight in the wondrous Dharma."
Thereupon he sighed and said:
“The Honored One among gods and men, the Tathāgata, is supreme;
with compassionate pity, he exhorts and rescues, bestowing his grace equally upon the three realms.”
For those of inferior, defiled, and impoverished conduct, gather them with the wealth of the Dharma;
cause all delusions to be explained away until no doubt remains.
Their bodies become honored and noble, endowed with peerless marks and signs of excellence.
He manifests his intent for the sake of others, expounding the Dharma without end.
His sagely wisdom flows in myriad streams, pouring forth like mountains and oceans;
the moisture of the Dharma nourishes the three realms, spreading throughout the ten directions.
The marks of a great man are perfected, and precious wisdom is fully endowed;
appearing in every place within the Dharma, he leads those who have not yet reached it.
His wisdom illuminates the darkness of ignorance, drawing them toward the pure realm.
"I vow that my body shall take refuge [in you] and reach the other shore.
Thereupon, after Shanhming had finished his praise, he stepped forward again, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Celestial Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will fulfill my original intention; today I have prepared a meal, and I only beg you to show compassion and deign to grace me with your presence."
The World-Honored One remained silent, as was his usual custom;
Shanming stood respectfully, believing he had not yet received permission.
Thereupon, Ānanda spoke to him, saying:
“The World-Honored One remained silent, which I take as his consent.
Having heard this, Shanming’s heart was filled with joy; he prostrated himself and departed, staying outside the gate and sending a messenger in to announce:
“I have now calculated my resources and find that I can provide a meal for two thousand people; I pray that you will inform the World-Honored One of this.”
Ānanda immediately informed the Buddha, recounting in full what Shanming had said.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Tell Shanming to return and provide the offerings, using everything you possess; the Buddha shall go with the entire assembly, so do not worry about the preparations being insufficient.”
Ānanda immediately went out and related everything to Shanming exactly as the Buddha had instructed.
Ānanda further said:
"Virtuous one, you may now return; do not entertain two thoughts or harbor fear that there may be insufficiency."
"Wherever the Buddha’s divine power reaches, nothing is not provided.
Shanming then stepped forward to prostrate before Ānanda and returned.
Upon returning home, he instructed his wife, children, and all members of the household, saying:
"The one we have now invited is titled the Celestial Honored One (Tianzun).
He is divinely wondrous and all-pervasive, possessing all-encompassing wisdom.
Whoever bestows even a single object upon such a person shall receive blessings in every lifetime without end."
Furthermore, he is able to deliver others and untie their knots.
You all should be reverent and solemn; provide pure offerings of food and drink, preparing a full array of flavors that are exquisitely delicious.
The attendants followed the messenger, each exerting their utmost heart and mind:
"A World-Honored One is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in hundreds of millions of kalpas; whatever must be done for him, let it be performed with perfect purity."
At that time, there was a wise man in the assembly named Balabhadra.
The Buddha commanded him to go and, together with Subhadra, provide offerings for this great assembly.

At that time, the twelve celestial kings, the four heavenly kings, and the Great Power Dragon King, receiving the Buddha’s instructions, all followed the powerful and accomplished masters of the various realms to go and assist him.
Upon their arrival, they greeted him with kind words, saying to Shanming:
"Worthy one, you have exerted yourself with diligence; the Buddha has sent us to provide you with assistance.
Shanming then stepped forward to pay homage to the Sages and the various Heavenly Kings, offering words of gratitude and respect.

“Venerable Sir, you have exerted yourself greatly; we have now prepared provisions for two thousand people. As the great assembly is about to arrive, I fear this small dwelling will not suffice—what shall we do?
Thereupon, the powerful masters of the assembly and the various deva-kings replied, “Do not worry.”
Thereupon, as they each looked around to the left and right, the chamber spontaneously became long, wide, high, and vast, like a celestial palace.
Beneath the roof, there were immediately thousands of billions of seats; the ground itself was transformed into these forms made of various jewels, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.
The beds and seats within the chamber were likewise so;
in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, there appeared hundreds of thousands of billions of people’s sets of food and utensils, all of which were sufficient and complete.
Various famous incenses were burned and silk banners were suspended; the path he traveled became broad and level.

Its color was like crystal, and rows of trees stood in formation. Natural music played with elegant sounds harmonizing most movingly, and the voice of the Dharma teaching possessed the eight qualities of the voices of Śakra and Brahmā.
At that time, the powerful and accomplished Sage of All Existence, along with the various heavenly kings, immediately returned to the Buddha’s presence.
Seeing this great transformation, Shanming was filled with wonder and joy; he leaped for gladness and approached the World-Honored One, saying:
“Having received the Buddha’s great compassion, all that has been prepared is now complete.”
"I only pray that you and the entire assembly will deign to honor us with your presence.
The Buddha then commanded King Ambara, the Wise Man, and six million others to lead the way, some traveling through the void.
The Buddha stood in the center, while the others followed behind him.

As the Tathāgata stepped out the gate, the earth shook with solemnity; the devas scattered flowers and burned various famous incenses, while celestial music was performed as they followed along, singing praises.

When they had all taken their seats, the heavenly kings and deities immediately assisted in serving the rice. The Buddha offered words of blessing, and after they had eaten until they were fully satisfied, the food did not diminish. The various vessels and utensils remained full as before.

Śubhamati thought to himself, “The World-Honored One’s majestic transformation is so vast and extensive! After he has finished eating and performed his ablutions, I shall inquire about the meaning of this.
When the water ablutions were completed, in the time it takes to extend one’s arm, the Buddha and the great assembly vanished in an instant and returned to sit within the vihāra.
Thereupon, Shanming again sighed in praise, saying:
"The World-Honored One is truly divine and wondrous, rarely seen or heard of in this world;
his transformations are extraordinary and sublime, such that all who behold him are filled with joy."
Contemplating this with deep attention, it is truly marvelous and sublime: manifesting transformations that are difficult to equal;
accomplished without effort, it spontaneously provides for all;
without speaking, it naturally exerts influence; without being commanded, beings act of their own accord.
Without acting, you encounter what is accomplished; by what means is this virtue sustained?
What fundamental practice or method did you employ, that at birth you possess such glory?
By accumulating what root of merit have you attained this towering and sublime dignity?
"I pray that you who pity this poor monk will open wide for me the wealth of the Dharma;
untie the net of my resolute doubts and release me so that no further uncertainty remains.
Having finished his praise, Shanming withdrew from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed him, saying:
"The place where I reside is not far from here; the village is named Fú'ān (Fu'an).
This is the very spot where the Buddha previously looked upon me with compassion.
While I was in that village, I was always fond of learning; I studied the worldly etiquette and the ancient royal codes, as well as the methods of the immortals and the sages."
"Recently, I heard that the World-Honored One resides near this country; I have begun to conceive images of him, and in my dreams, he has appeared in a semblance of his true form.
A disciple of the World-Honored One named Śāriputra frequently comes to my house and preaches the Dharma for me."
The Dharma is profoundly subtle and wondrous; it is something I have long hoped to hear. Though my heart rejoices and praises it, I still harbor a sense of confusion.

Today I have come lightly to pay homage to the Buddha, the Honored One of Heaven, and to observe the Way and its teachings. Following what I ought to practice, I have attained a joy of mind, like one beholding light in the darkness.
I intended to prepare a meal, but having encountered an extraordinary inquiry, I was hesitant to speak for fear that what I possessed was too meager.

The World-Honored One, through his supernormal powers, anticipated my thoughts; aided by his spiritual strength, the seats and the food were suddenly prepared. When the meal was finished, the vessels remained full as before.
"What kind of transformation is this?
How marvelous and wondrous it is!
Furthermore, I observe the World-Honored One’s thirty-two marks; each mark possesses its own excellence, and one never tires of beholding them."
In walking, he was composed and orderly, neither too slow nor too fast;
in sitting, he sat in the center, neither forward nor backward;
his speech consisted of eight qualities, neither sluggish nor hurried.
His words have established the laws and regulations, and his clear admonitions are as bright as the sun, causing all beings to receive his grace and blessings.
What deeds did he perform in the past that he was born with such [qualities]?

"Furthermore, I see the World-Honored One’s feet do not touch the ground; the marks on his soles are clearly defined, and he is as dignified and majestic as a painting. His body is empty and light, manifesting transformations wherever he goes. By what practices did he attain these? How does he come to possess such qualities in this world?"
"I pray that you will deign to explain this, so that I may understand its beginning and end.
Thereupon, the Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"As you have asked, the Tathāgata shall explain it in full. Compose your hearts and minds, and all receive this teaching without forgetting.
Shanming then said, "I accept your instruction."
The Buddha said:

"In the past, I first practiced the conduct of the six virtues, never abandoning them from lifetime to lifetime. It was by this means that I attained Buddhahood, achieving mastery over transformations at will; whatever I do, I am omniscient, reaching understanding of all things."
He then asked:
"What are called the practices of the six virtues?
He replied:
“Vast giving, vast precepts, vast patience, vast diligence, vast single-mindedness, and vast wisdom.
He then asked the Buddha Bhagavān clearly:
“What is meant by ‘vast giving’?”
The Buddha said:

"One who practices the Way must first understand that the body is not a permanent or true entity; it is composed of the four great elements, consisting of bones, flesh, and impurities, all of which must eventually be cast aside and return to their original source, for it cannot abide forever."
The body is not mine; wealth and possessions are not permitted to me; the mind has no form, and one thoroughly understands that names are impermanent.
Bound by the conditions of dependent origination, there is thus bodily activity; yet the body is without permanence and shall likewise become empty and decay.
Reflecting in this manner, one establishes the four reliances:

that both the internal body and the external body, as well as heaven, earth, and the myriad things, are all without permanence; they must eventually return to ruin and decay, being cast aside, dispersed, and dissolved.

Once this faith is established, one contemplates that the essence is neither existent nor non-existent, and that phenomena are neither substantial entities nor non-entities; thus, one is able to bestow gifts freely, satisfying others.
Furthermore, through the gift of Dharma, one transforms and guides the ignorant and deluded; therefore, it is called "extensive giving."
"What is meant by 'extensive precepts'?
He replied:
"The extensive precepts refer to being able to restrain the three calamities of the body, guard against the four faults of the mouth, and check the three evils of the mind."

Regarding physical conduct: if one sees any sentient beings, even those crawling or wriggling, one should feel compassion and pity for them, release them to live, and return them to safety according to their needs, whether on water or land.

If one sees various precious jewels or objects that are soft, smooth, and pleasing to the mind, even though one's own body suffers from poverty, one should subdue the mind within and not allow greed to take hold.

Furthermore, upon seeing subtle forms adorned with cosmetics and fragrant powders, one internally contemplates their decay, putrefaction, and the stench of pus and blood; these are the three precepts for the body.

As for the practice of speech: if another should inflict the four faults upon oneself, one recognizes the failure of one's own speech and responds with kind words and gentle discourse—sincere and unadorned—answering so as to transform them, causing them to turn back and follow one's example; these are the four precepts for the mouth.

As for the practice of the mind, one cultivates wisdom within the heart, contemplates birth and death, and dwells perpetually in the realm of insight, remaining undeluded amidst the turbid flow of existence.
Furthermore, one deeply enters the essentials of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and emptiness, discerning the true and the conventional without doubt or difficulty.
To encourage others upon seeing them do good, and to rejoice on their behalf when they achieve success—these are the three precepts of intention.

Thus, at the beginning of practicing the Way, one first observes the ten precepts; being able to practice them oneself and further transforming others, one exerts effort without slackening and acts without ceasing, harboring no thought of weariness whatsoever. Therefore, it is called the "Universal Precept."
"What is meant by 'vast patience'?
He replied:
"Vast patience means that if someone reviles me, I calculate that the sound arises from the voice and comes here; yet upon observation, it is found to have no form."
The source from which these original sounds arise is the mind and intention; yet when one contemplates the mind and intention, they likewise have no form.

Examining that upon which the mind relies, it relies upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); when these four elements return to their origin, they are then nameless, neither "self" nor "other," neither male nor female, and neither old nor young—calculating thus, one finds there is no master.
Wherever there is shame, it has no form and yet is given a name.
Within these two absences, there is likewise no form; when these three are reckoned together, they are empty and non-existent.

When the wise person contemplates and reflects in this manner with a detached mind, anger does not arise; through the patience of emptiness regarding emptiness, they further endure all evils and refrain from committing them.

"When an offense occurs, one does not give rise to anger; one examines the mind and subdues the will, being able to do so oneself and also instructing others to do the same—this is called 'extensive patience.
What is meant by 'extensive diligence'?"
"Reduce excessive eating and do not relish flavors;
eliminate sleep and remain vigilant day and night.
Distance yourself from the mundane and draw near to the Way, practicing the various precepts."
Regarding the methods of sitting and rising, one should not lose proper decorum; regarding conduct free from transgression, one should cultivate it within the mind.
As for the essentials of the factors of the path, one should zealously delight in reciting them, diligently receiving instruction by day and practicing walking meditation by night.
His speech conforms to the Vinaya; body, mouth, and mind act in unison. He follows the mindfulness of the Dharma and does not depart from the scriptural texts.
Seated, he expounds extensively; his mind is not weary, and he enlightens the ignorant and stubborn without succumbing to indolence or fatigue.
"To oppose one's own inclinations and turn back from one's habitual thoughts, to apply oneself with single-minded dedication, and having attained mastery in the body, to further instruct others—
this is called 'extensive diligence.
What is meant by 'extensive single-mindedness'?"
"To serve one's parents with filial piety, one unifies the mind;
to honor and respect teachers and friends, one unifies the mind;
to sever attachment and distance oneself from the mundane world, one unifies the mind."
Entering the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they unify their mind;
dwelling in empty stillness and solitude, they unify their mind;
amidst the clamor and confusion of the multitude, they unify their mind.
Amidst much desire and much contention, amidst much doing and much affliction, one should unify the mind in this state;
amidst praise and slander, gain and loss, and matters of good and evil, one should remain unshaken and unify the mind;
by counting the breaths and entering dhyāna, abandoning the six [sense objects] to attain purity, one should unify the mind.
"To personally practice it and further teach others—this is called 'extensive single-mindedness.
What is meant by 'extensive wisdom'?
He replied:

“The wise man, according to the body he receives, encounters three kinds of suffering, six afflictions, the defilement of the five obscurations, sixty-two types of hesitant thoughts, eighty-eight difficult-to-unravel bonds, and eighteen hundred pains like sharp wounds.”
Regarding these matters, one uses wisdom to understand each one clearly:
observing their arising and examining their cessation;
viewing their ailments and selecting the appropriate medicine.
Having grasped these essentials, one ensures that the body does not violate the precepts and the mind does not enter the secular world.
While dwelling amidst the affection of the multitude, the mind remains within the treasury of the factors of enlightenment;
though lodging in the house of the six afflictions, the mind dwells in the hall of the six purities.
Dwelling in a chamber of the five obscurations, the mind dwells at the threshold of cessation;
leaning against a house of instability, the mind contemplates the protection of skillful means;
sitting upon the ground of venomous serpents, the mind ponders the path of relinquishment and distancing.
Riding upon the peril of a wrecked boat, one’s mind plots the path to self-salvation;
approaching a forest ablaze with fierce fire, one’s mind seeks the security of extinguishing it with water.
Therefore, the enlightened person employs the skillful means of wisdom to extricate themselves from the hardships of birth and death.
To sever all conceptualizations of the three realms and proceed to the ground of extinction—
practicing this oneself and also teaching others— is what is meant by the meaning of the six virtues of extensive wisdom.
"As to what you have asked regarding the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations, marks and signs, and immeasurable virtues—how does he attain them?

By practicing these six dharmas, as well as the various wisdoms and concentrations, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the boundless and bottomless practices of dhāraṇī, he has attained the title of Buddha and the status of World-Honored One, such that there is nothing he cannot accomplish."
Thereupon, Shanming and the entire assembly, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, all raised their voices and made a vow to give rise to the supreme, peerless, and impartial mind.
They all said, "Today we have attained great merit; may all people swiftly attain this practice.

At that time, Shanming attained the four purities: first, purity of the eyes; second, purity of the body; third, purity of speech; and fourth, purity of the mind. Joyfully bowing his head, he silently contemplated the meaning of the Dharma.
Thereupon, Shanming withdrew from his seat, knelt with his knees on the ground, and addressed the Tathāgata, saying:

"The teachings spoken by the World-Honored One are vast and boundless; the prohibitions of the Dharma are subtle and profound. They restrain and govern the mind and its states, subduing the heart until it attains purity, whereby calamities and defilements are extinguished. For one who merely hears this, the merit is already great; how much more so for one who puts it into practice—their virtue would be difficult to measure."

The Celestial Honored One further said: "In previous lives, they did not merely practice these six matters; they also practiced the methods of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *dhāraṇīs*, and the boundless thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Thus, they accomplished the complete Buddha-deeds, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the ten powers (*bala*), and the eighteen unique and wondrous dharmas. Their transformations were sovereign, their speech was without difficulty, and they beheld the Buddhas face-to-face. Flying to the ten directions, they bestowed [the Dharma] upon all who had not yet been saved, leading and transforming them through deliverance.

They destroyed the storehouses of evil and guided those who were crooked and perverse. Within the midst of suffering, they gave rise to existence without attachment or cessation; by means of this non-attachment and non-cessation, they performed the practices of causes and conditions to instruct all who were deluded."
Such are these wondrous virtues and their countless modes of practice; by what meditative concentration are they attained?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will expound their profound meaning for the sake of those in the present and the future, so that they may achieve liberation.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"What you wish to ask, I shall now analyze for you, fully expounding the essential points; compose your mind and listen well.
He replied, "I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said:
“There is a meditative state called ‘Accomplished Radiance.
If there are those who hear of it and are able to practice it for one day up to seven days, its merit and blessings are beyond comparison.”

Those who hear this Dharma have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in previous lives; having heard it at their very seats, they did not doubt it, and thus in this life they have once again encountered this Dharma of the Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance.

Now that you have attained the practice of this cultivation, even for as brief a moment as a finger-snap, you shall be forever separated from the three evil realms; your merit will gradually become full, and you will swiftly reach Buddhahood.
All the matters you previously asked about will be completely accomplished.
Śubhaprabha asked:
"By practicing how many things does one attain this noble concentration?
The Buddha said:
"One must purify oneself through one hundred and thirty-five matters before one can enter this samādhi:

distancing oneself from bodily conduct, departing from verbal transgressions, eliminating mental intentions, exhausting the three impurities, repelling the six afflictions, and blocking the five obscurations; having completely cast off the twelve links of dependent origination, untied the knots, and clarified the sixty-two types of speculative views."

He heals many wounds, delights those who are distressed, relinquishes all greatness, discards bone and blood, avoids kin, severs all habits, cuts off craving, is free from both the acceptable and the unacceptable, scrapes away the defilement of greed, harvests the roots of desire, is not deluded by the current, can restrain illness, does not reckon in terms of self, and is without the notion of "not-self. He establishes the four kinds of faith, abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, advances toward the four right efforts, plants the five faculties, practices the five powers, understands the seven factors of enlightenment, treads the eightfold path, enters the eight recollections, and exerts the eight constant diligences. Having thus attained that for which there is no further effort to be made, he departs from what cannot be practiced.

One studies superior wisdom, honors one's own mind, and is neither arrogant nor fickle; one rains down the rain of Dharma. Regarding a single dharma, one does not calculate it as two, does not conceive of it as three, does not form notions of what is useless, has no notion of limits, does not form notions of emptiness, does not form notions of non-existence, forms the notion of nowhere, and does not dwell upon the notion of nowhere.

He skillfully contemplates that the Buddha knows the purity of the Buddha; having known that purity, he trains well, his mind abides correctly, and he does not regress into error. He treats good and evil as equal, regarding light and darkness as identical; knowing that both light and darkness are empty, he harbors no doubt regarding the Dharma, nor does he conceive of purity as existing or non-existing. He contemplates that existence and non-existence are fundamentally one.

Having known one thing and removed another, he does not give rise to conceptualization regarding that one thing; he diligently receives the teaching, skillfully practices it, and through such practice enters the boundless; he cultivates superior intention, does not listen to the mind, skillfully guards consciousness, and does not allow it to wander distractedly.

Coming and going three times without attachment, examining all natures and realizing they have no root; knowing that what has no root cannot be fulfilled, one maintains self-discipline through this non-fulfillment.

Observing phenomena thread by thread as being identical to emptiness, abiding eternally without cessation or conceptualization, transcending permanence and impermanence; not dwelling on persons, not indulging in the world, not clinging to things, and ceasing all seeking; harmonizing with the Dharma through detachment and being free from views; understanding that birth and death of the body are all transformations; and knowing that the Dharma is equal across the superior, middling, and inferior—thus one proceeds from this life to future lives.

"Contemplate the two causes as being like empty space; let the mind be free from desire yet ever benevolent. Practice purity and skillfully guide others. Knowing that people turn toward turbidity, remain clear and limpid amidst that turbidity. Let the mind distance itself from craving as one would enter fire with a sinew; burn away all defilements with the pure fire. Once defilements are exhausted, one is tranquil and pure. One does not dwell on good nor dwell on evil; one does not contemplate the beautiful nor the ugly; one does not dwell on suffering nor dwell on pleasure. Regarding blame or praise, there is neither joy nor anger. With a mind tamed and pure, one enters wherever one goes. Opening the great treasury, one enters the Great Dharma; protecting the fullness of the Dharma through the discipline of the Path, one diligently and earnestly practices the truth of suffering and its origin."

Taking the perfection of the Way as its radiance, one observes the arising of all natures and consciousnesses; when the flow of entanglements and the obscurity of mental intentions cease, one diligently seeks cessation to enter the Way.

He has cut off the three cravings, eliminated the four losses, increased the four cities, departed from the five veils, severed the six types of pride, cultivated the six respects, and attained the realization of the six dharmas. He practices the seven wisdoms, strengthens the eight powers, uproots the nine fetters, and trains in the nine cessations. Having perfected the ten vast purities as his own capability, he is fully endowed with the wisdom of the ten powers; having no more to learn regarding the ten upright dharmas, the seeds of wisdom and dharma remain ever-present. Having already perfected the Three Jewels, he bestows the Dharma-gift without end. In all matters, he is capable of perfect practice; he enters non-attachment, enters emptiness without weariness, casts away the notion of self, is free from the thought of "I," is without reckoning of persons, and is without calculation—tranquil as if in *nirvāṇa*.
"This constitutes the practice of the precepts for the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance, consisting of one hundred and thirty-five matters.

When the Buddha had spoken this Chapter on the Precepts for the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance, three hundred thousand luminous beings attained the merit of this samādhi and were established in the tenth stage.

Śubhaprabha attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); his five hundred companions were filled with joy and delight, and they all resolved their minds upon the supreme, peerless, and equal enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Four hundred thousand wise ones (vidvāṃsaḥ) all established themselves in the practice of non-retrogression.
Fifty thousand members of the assembly who had abandoned evil all attained the path of non-attachment (asaṅga-mārga).
Two thousand virtuous men and women who observed the five precepts all attained the practice of the tracks of the noble ones (āryapudgala-caryā).
The devas in the void of space played musical instruments and exclaimed:
"How wonderful!
How delightful!"

The people of the world have now attained the essential point of the supreme teaching; as for those who were ignorant, dull-witted, and defiled by dust, today they have been suddenly and completely cleansed.
Just as impurities are washed away by pure water, so too, having heard the Great Dharma today, the defilements of their minds have been eliminated.
We pray that the Wheel of Dharma may turn perpetually, so that all may swiftly attain wondrous wisdom.
May we always encounter the World-Honored One, never being separated from him in whatever realm we are born.
May we quickly attain this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance, and widely proclaim the grace of the Dharma to illuminate and dispel the darkness once more.
"At this great assembly today, we shall establish countless foundations of the Way.

Shanming bowed to the Buddha and said, "Now that I have heard the World-Honored One’s resolve, I have purified my mind and reflected within myself. I observe my own lack of wisdom; I do not know its location, whether it is external or internal—it is likewise so in both cases."
The Buddha told Shanming:

"It is like entering a dark room while holding a torch; one no longer perceives where the darkness lies. In the same way, when one practices the dharma of meditative concentration and is able to fulfill the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), one no longer perceives the loss caused by the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda) rooted in ignorance."
"Excellent, Śubhaprabha!

It is not merely this; one does not perceive the places where birth-and-death arises and ceases throughout the ten directions. This extends to those who have reached the state of non-attachment in their traces, the pratyekabuddhas awakened through causes and conditions, and even up to the Tathāgata—all are without seeing, for whatever is perceived as having an object of thought is not true seeing."

To have no perception, to have the perception of universal purity, to have the perception of cessation-purity, and yet not to have the perception of cessation-purity—this is the view of emptiness in which there is nothing seen.
Subhapati addressed the World-Honored One:
"In what sense is it said that not ceasing the perception of purity constitutes the view of emptiness?
At that time, where does the mind abide?"
"What do you see?
The Buddha said,
"Śubhaprabha!"

At that time, the mind is not within, nor does it abide without; it is not in the Path, nor in the mundane; it is not in existence, nor in non-existence; it is not in arising, nor in ceasing, nor in any state of movement.
This mind has no root-limit and no sound; having thoroughly investigated its beginning and end, one should view it in this way.
This viewing is viewing, it is emptiness, it is cessation, and it is the state of meditative concentration wherein nothing at all exists.
Regarding this view, a wise person should form this reflection: "I shall eliminate these thoughts and attain purity.
One who forms such a reflection acts in accordance with the teaching for accomplishing the meditative concentration of radiant light.
Because these dharmas are dharmas that do not exist, their names are established by force of convention.

When a wise person hears this, they should feel neither alarm nor doubt; rather, they should contemplate these dharmas with precision, remaining neither regressive nor indolent. This constitutes having already attained the power of protection through the majestic spiritual authority of concentrated mind.
“Śubhaprabha!
Those who wish to study this should practice four matters and gradually enter the state of non-seeing. He said:
“What are the four?
First, the absence of a body; second, the absence of a dwelling; third, the absence of a world; fourth, the absence of things.”
"One who is able to do so shall attain entry into the four essentials.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"What are the four essentials?"
He replied:
"First is the essential of the Buddha; second is the essential of the Dharma; third is the essential of emptiness; and fourth is the essential of cessation.
These are called the four essentials."
The Buddha then uttered this verse of praise:
“Without that notion of self, yet not lacking wise discernment;
Unattached to the twelve links of dependent origination— This is how one should achieve fulfillment.”
This concentration is fundamentally non-existent, having no place where it abides;
out of compassion for the world its name is manifested, and its practice in emptiness accords with the proper ritual.
The human mind and the mental consciousness—these three are the dharmas that arise.
Practicing this, one achieves fulfillment; there is neither arising nor cessation.
Emptiness is the ground of fulfillment; the suffering of birth and death is severed and abandoned.
When all things leave no further trace, this is the practice of concentration in accord with the mind.
Worldlings rely upon one another, clinging to false views and famous dharmas;
Craving gain and harboring constant delusions, they are bound and fettered through countless lifetimes.
Their accumulated practices are perpetually obstructed; they are beset by sorrow and distress, their minds shrouded in grief.
The four transformations follow like shadows, coming and going without rest.
Practicing concentration without dependence, one observes correctly and does not cling to names;
when craving is exhausted and conceptualization ceases, one is liberated from bonds, pure and at peace.
Pure conduct is free from delusion; the afflictions of the mind are utterly non-existent.
Birth, old age, and sickness have been severed; there is no longer the sorrow of coming and going.
The eye of wisdom is already vast and bright; the root of knowledge is without limit or bottom.
The wise one practices the perfection of crossing over; by practicing meditative concentration, he attains this state.

The brilliance of the fire-star and the moon, the radiance of the sun and Mount Kunlun, and the light illuminating the palaces of Śakra and Brahmā—all these are surpassed by the clarity of this concentration.
The Buddha told Shanming:
"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King Who Subdues Desire.

At that time, the Buddha’s lifespan in the world was one hundred thousand years; he did not reside here in South India, but rather at the place where the Buddha currently dwells, in the Pure Radiance Heaven (Vimalaprabhā) to the north. That land is reached after passing through three hundred million buddha-fields."

Venerable one, when the Buddha King Subduer of Desire appeared, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years; he constantly had six hundred thousand disciples following him, and the assembly of wise men (*vidvats*) was beyond calculation.

The people were flourishing, abundant, and peaceful; they were all virtuous in conduct, their moral precepts and virtues towering high, while the three stains of desire and greed were thin and suppressed.

At that time, the Buddha convened a great assembly of enlightened sages from the ten directions and universally taught and upheld this Samādhi of Perfect Radiance. Thereby, he fulfilled his buddha-work, which was counted among the four stations.
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Prajñādṛśa, who was five hundred years old; yet the people of the land regarded him as a youth.
When Prajñādṛśa heard of the Buddha’s great assembly, he petitioned his parents, requesting permission to go to the Buddha to observe his deeds.

Having received permission from her parents, she went at once to see the Buddha. She prostrated herself on the ground; having completed her salutation, she stood upright with a heart overflowing with joy. She then removed the precious, exquisite, and variegated jeweled necklaces from her person and scattered them over the Buddha.

Through the Buddha’s divine majesty, those scattered ornaments were instantly transformed into flower canopies, which reached out to cover the great assembly, each person having their own distinct one.
The Buddha bade him take a seat and expounded for him the dharma of this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance. His heart was further filled with joy, and he then made this vow:
"May I always encounter this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance in every life I am born into, may I be able to practice it swiftly, and may I never let my virtue of the precepts decline."
At that time, the youth bestowed all his treasures as alms and made a single, ultimate vow; by virtue of this, he was able to receive [rebirth] in every world in which he was born.
"Śubhaprabha!
Do you know who that youth was at that time?
It was none other than yourself."
Now that I have appeared in the world, you have again encountered this concentrated mind.
From this day forward, you shall surely attain it before long;
after attaining wisdom, two hundred kalpas hence, you shall become a fully enlightened Buddha named King Who Guides the World.
"The One Most Honored Above Heaven and Below Heaven shall now transform and guide those who are ignorant and deluded, as I do now.

Upon hearing the Buddha bestow upon him this name for his investiture, Shanming’s mind became pure and his body light, like lapis lazuli or crystal, clean within and without, entirely free of defilement. As he purified his mind in every place where he stayed, he subsequently attained the ten states of sublime tranquility (*daśa-dharmāḥ praśrabdhayaḥ*).

First, to be serene and unmoved by what one sees; second, to be serene and ever content amidst all wearying affairs; third, to be serene and free from conceptualization amidst manifold thoughts; fourth, to be serenely satiated in renouncing the urgent pursuits that worldly folk delight in; fifth, to be serene and neither mindful of seeking nor mindful of rejecting regarding virtue and non-virtue; sixth, to be serene and unattached to both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; seventh, to be serene and not hope for honor from the humble or the worthy; eighth, to be serene and free from joy or anger regarding respect, support, or their abandonment; ninth, to be serene and view all things—whether in accord with the Dharma or contrary to it—as identical in their fundamental source; tenth, when entering pure stillness or remaining in impurity, to be able to transform others through the Dharma, being serene and without notions of attachment or aversion, or of rejection or abandonment.
With such thoughts in his mind, he addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!

You have now bestowed upon me the essentials of this consecration. I shall repay your kindness by proclaiming and opening it up for all, so that those who have not heard may hear, those who do not know may know, and those who have not been delivered may be delivered."
My births and deaths have been constant and numerous; though they are many and long-lasting, I do not consider them a weariness.

Being unattached, awakened, capable of self-composure, free from delusion, and able to enter into their manifestations, I reveal them according to causes and conditions. I do not regard my own births and deaths as mere births and deaths; having received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I have fully and completely understood them all.

I have a retinue of five hundred people; I pray that the World-Honored One will extend his fourfold great compassion to us, endeavoring to lead us into the Dharma and causing us to quickly understand this Samādhi of the Perfectly Accomplished Radiance.

Thereupon the Buddha smiled, and light issued from his mouth, brilliant in five colors, its radiance reaching the ten directions—those who were in pain all attained peace at once—and the light returned to enter through the crown of his head, resuming its usual luster.
The attendant Ānanda adjusted his robes, withdrew from his seat, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
“The Buddha has never rejoiced or smiled without cause; this smile must surely have a reason.
I only pray that you will expound upon it and reveal what we have not yet heard.”
Thereupon Ānanda uttered this verse of praise:
“The countenance of the Hero among Men, With eyes, nose, and mouth perfectly upright;
The golden body is exceedingly supple and delicate— Why do you smile with such great joy?”
With a square face and white teeth, lips as bright as glowing embers;
endowed with the eighty marks of beauty, there must surely be a cause for this smile now.
Forty teeth like mirrors, a broad tongue, and square jawbones.
When you speak, a fragrant scent is emitted; for whom is this present smile intended?
Your eyebrows and mustache are a deep azure-blue, and the two parts of your eyelids are perfectly symmetrical;
a white tuft of hair stands between your brows like a celestial mark—now that you smile, we pray only to hear its cause.
The celestial eye is already clear and bright; the Dharma-eye is already fully attained.
The Dharma-eye and the wisdom-eye—these four are now perfected.
A smile is always accompanied by a response, initiating transformation for those who have not yet reached completion.
"Perhaps he shall receive the prediction of his future attainment; therefore, he smiles with his golden countenance.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The Buddha truly does not smile without cause!"

The five hundred worthy men who now follow Shanming had already made offerings to two hundred billion Buddhas in previous lives. While sitting in their presence, they heard these one hundred and thirty-five lines from within the *Sūtra of the Perfectly Accomplished Radiant Wisdom*. Although many lifetimes have passed since they first heard them, they have remained consistently rigid and fierce, merely ranking among those of minor virtue; they have not yet been able to subdue their minds to receive and uphold this pure and most wondrous practice of meditative concentration.
Nevertheless, by virtue of having heard this, one will not be reborn in the three evil realms and will always encounter and meet with this sublime and definitive Dharma.
Having come to this assembly today, listen with a pure mind; I shall gradually explain and elucidate it so that you may enter the True Truth.
Afterwards, when the Buddha Maitreya appears, at that time they shall attain this Samādhi of Perfect Radiance.
Thirty-six trillion kalpas hence, they shall all become Buddhas.

Furthermore, they shall transform and teach by means of these dharmas; the lands they govern each have their own names: the first is named King of the Radiant Array of Banners and Banners, the second is named Great Light Pervasively Manifesting, the third is named Great Power Subduing Evil, the fourth is named Fierce and Majestic Virtue, the fifth is named Pure Sound of Flowing Water, the sixth is named Universal Reception of Noble Virtue, the seventh is named Manifesting Splendor to Eliminate Knots, and the eighth is named Sovereign Transformation of Illusions—each having such a name.

Thereupon, having heard the pronouncement of their future enlightenment, the five hundred worthy men were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they immediately attained five kinds of unswerving resolve:
first, the resolve that seeking merit through sacrificial offerings shall not cause them to waver;

second, the resolve that among all the various flavors, whether acceptable or otherwise, these are all the vital essence of sentient beings' spirits, and they shall never waver as to refraining from using what is edible to harm living creatures.
Third, they correctly establish themselves in the practice of the unsurpassed and solitary honor, never wavering or turning away to pursue inferior paths;

fourth, knowing that this Dharma is supreme and without equal, they practice with diligent mind, recognizing that although there may be other teachings, they are merely diverse and empty distractions, and through the discernment of their Dharma-mind, they never turn away from it;

fifth, whether there are Buddhas in the world or not, whether the Dharma flourishes or declines, and whether it has an end or is severed, their minds remain fixed in meditative concentration, and they do not turn toward wrong actions because these Three Jewels are absent.
These are the five minds that do not regress.
Having attained these dharmas and their meanings, they all knelt on their right knees before the World-Honored One and said to him:
"May the Buddha have compassion for us!"
He informed them of his name upon being consecrated as a Buddha, saying, "We shall repay his kindness.

In the future, if we are born into an age of corruption and evil, we shall diligently cultivate right practice and propagate the Honored Dharma. We shall transform those who do not yet understand; we shall rectify the chaotic, rouse the indolent, encourage the retreating, support the faltering, restore what is deficient or fearful, illuminate the obscure, and untie the knots."

For those who kill, he explains the calamity of an untimely death; for those who steal, he explains the suffering of poverty and begging; for those who commit sexual misconduct, he explains the misfortunes of the body; for those who slander, flatter, or deceive, he explains the affliction of losing one's nature; and for those who are intoxicated and disorderly, he explains the perilous changes that endanger the person.
Today, before the Buddha, we together make a vow of five aspirations: to practice the conduct of a wise man until the attainment of Buddhahood, continuing without ceasing.
We pray that the Buddha will have compassion for us!
Listen to what we say.
"Our first vow is this:
having practiced the conduct of a vidyādhara, may we swiftly cause our bodies to undergo transformations and circulate throughout the ten directions."
If there were no Buddha in the world, some among the fourfold assembly who understand the Dharma might say:
"It is truly certain that a Buddha exists, but he has entered parinirvāṇa!
When worldly people with false views give rise to the net of doubt, seeing neither the Buddha nor his knowledge of the Dharma, they will then say:
"There is no Buddha; it is merely a false fabrication!
If there truly were a Buddha, why do we not see his majestic spiritual power?
Thus they disputed with one another.

When they are in dispute, I shall go there to transform them, manifesting the Buddha’s body with its marks and signs to illuminate them, and further manifesting my majestic spiritual power so that it may be seen before those two disputants, causing them to know truly that the Buddha exists, and saying to them:
"Do not harbor doubt!"

The person who harbors such doubts shall immediately experience both surprise and joy; for him, the Buddha will preach the Dharma to teach and deliver him, and having done so, will vanish through transformation—thus it is infinite.
"The second vow is: The Buddha possesses great, wondrous, and most profound immeasurable Dharma-gates, the essentials of the twelve divisions of the scriptures."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples each studied a single sūtra and were biased toward one fascicle; unable to be universally proficient, and not yet understanding the equality of the four types of teachings and skillful means, they proceeded to challenge and refute one another.

Some speak of emptiness, while others speak of existence; some say that a certain meaning is thus, while others say it is not so. Those who truly understand the meaning of the Dharma focus on the nature of words and expressions, whereas those who do not comprehend the meaning are greedy for names and terminology. They adorn their outward appearances as if they were fully realized, and thus, within the assembly, they engage in mutual disputes, giving rise to anger and abandoning the good for the evil.

When there is such a dispute, I shall go and manifest a physical transformation that surpasses all others, causing the assembly to become solemn; I will then deliver a decisive discourse to distinguish what is correct from what is not.
He draws upon the sutras to provide explanations that cause both parties to rejoice; having done so, he vanishes through transformation, and thus [his activity] is infinite.
"The third vow is:

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when laypeople or those of external wisdom enter among the great assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, and the disciples discuss the meaning of the Dharma, speaking of various paths, distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, or grading them by high and low, they shall then say: [text continues]"
"Among the ninety-six kinds of paths, the Buddha is the most honored!
He possesses the four bases of spiritual power for flying and transformation; in all that is above and below heaven, there is no one whose wisdom equals that of the Buddha."

Worldly scholars, having been born without beholding a Buddha and being habituated to false views, believe in the Lesser Vehicle while disparaging the Greater; they then say to the disciples of the Buddha:

"Do not speak falsely, claiming that the Buddha possesses supernatural powers, flying through the air, and performing transformations. From ancient times until now, among the various classes of human beings, no such thing has ever existed."
"These are not sincere or truthful words.

At that time, I transformed myself into the physical form of a Buddha, manifesting all the various marks of excellence and displaying supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). I walked upon the air and emitted fire and water from my body, causing the laypeople and those learned in external teachings to be struck with solemn awe and wonder, so that they might recognize the transformation wrought by majestic spiritual power.
He preached the Dharma for them and bestowed upon them the true precepts; having finished, he passed away into transformation, continuing thus without end.
"The fourth vow is:
If there are people who read and recite the Buddhist sutras while staying alone in a wilderness dwelling, or among the mountains, or within a great kingdom."
The noble clansmen, elders, and the common people lacked a teacher and the Dharma; some had unclear teachers, while others were stubborn and had no one to question, their minds ensnared by doubt.

I transformed myself into a practitioner, donned the robes, and went to where they were; I explained it for them word by word until the beginning and end were fully distinguished, their doubts were skillfully dispelled, and they were led to enter the subtle and wondrous state beyond all difficulty or hesitation.
Having done so, he immediately vanished;
such was his boundless power. "The fifth vow is:
in whatever land I am born, may I always encounter a Buddha."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples established shrines, fashioned images and statues of the Buddha, and constructed lecture halls where they discussed the sutras and the Dharma.
As for worldly people, they opened schools to cultivate meager wisdom, yet remained bound by the four inversions.

Upon hearing the disciples of the Buddha expound upon the Dharma for transcending the world and the essentials for escaping birth and death, they immediately go to challenge and reject them; failing to appreciate what is authentic and true, they slander, revile, and disparage it. Driven by a desire for fame and victory, or even harboring resentment and anger, they seek to destroy and ruin it, insulting, scorning, and belittling it with contempt, thereby obstructing the True Path so that it cannot be practiced.
At that time, I shall manifest the body of a Buddha and preach the most sublime Dharma for them once more.

I will manifest the retributions of birth and death, calamity and fortune; I will lead them to the heavens to observe the mansions of merit, and I will lead them to the hells to witness the retribution for their transgressions.
He strikes them with the majesty of the Dharma and subdues them with the power of wisdom, causing them to immediately submit and faithfully embrace the Great Way.
Having done so, he then departs through transformation; such is his boundless [power].
"From the time I become an enlightened sage until I attain Buddhahood, I shall always practice these five vows without ceasing.
We pray that the World-Honored One, by the merit of his great compassion, will protect and bless us, enabling us to fulfill our aspirations."
Thereupon the Buddha said:
"Excellent is this aspiration!
This is what a wise man should resolve upon; from this day forward, you shall surely attain it without loss."
"You should simply always guard your conduct so that it is not corrupted or leaked.
Diligently lead all beings, and you shall swiftly attain your aspiration.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"The Great Mind first gives rise to the vow; through these five, it transforms delusions.
It shall bring to fruition countless beings, and those who doubt shall enter the Way.
This virtue is immeasurable, the foremost among all practices."
If a person hears this vow, the net of doubt shall be forever eliminated.
These five vows constitute the stage of Buddhahood; that which is subdued therein accords with the transformation of the Way.
Great wisdom is nothing superior to this; this vow is the highest among men.
"Five hundred worthy gentlemen have made vows equal to those of the Twin [Śāla] Trees;
in future lives they shall not lose them, and all shall receive blessings and joy.
The Buddha then addressed the worthy gentlemen and all those present in the assembly:

"This Dharma is the ultimate truth; it should be well-practiced. One should take the fulfillment of its requirements as the foundation, for empty talk and flowery speech are not in accord with the Dharma."

One should practice forbearance and refrain from evil, whether in seclusion or among the great assembly of high and low. Internally restraining the mind, one should act in accordance with the precepts;
one must not commit transgressions through idle entertainment, nor be arrogant in the midst of a gathering, nor be haughty and conceited because of one’s high status.
One does not waver or follow others because of being lowly or weak;
one feels no shame for good and no shame for evil;
and one does not plant seeds of what is unbeneficial.
The mind is like the True Dharma, without wavering;
it does not give rise to thoughts of increase or decrease.
Such an enlightened person will surely attain their aspirations through the five vows of the roots of goodness and swiftly achieve supreme Buddhahood.
At that time, the noble King Vimalarāja rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One:

“I pray that today the Buddha will manifest the majestic spiritual power of this Samādhi of Perfectly Complete Radiance, so that this assembly may behold it with joy and delight, and all may resolve to establish the roots of virtue—those who have not yet attained completion shall complete it, and those who have not yet crossed over shall cross over.”
At that time, among those seated there was a wise man named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The Buddha praised Mahāsthāmaprāpta, saying:
"Manifest now the majestic spiritual power of this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance."

Immediately accepting the instruction, he remained seated without rising or moving; entering a state of meditative concentration through wisdom with a spirit of profound stillness, in the mere twinkling of an eye, all the small mountains, great mountains, major barriers, and minor barriers within the trichiliocosm were entirely extinguished and no longer appeared, becoming universally level and the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, he caused all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to be mutually visible to one another, with each being at a distance of only one fathom.
When observing the seats where the Buddhas of the ten directions sit, it was as if looking up at the constellations of stars—beyond calculation.

Furthermore, with his right hand, he lifted up all the Buddhas of the ten directions and their three thousand great thousandfold world systems, placing them upon a single fingertip and lowering them again, as easily as lifting a single speck of dust.
Among the people therein, including even the wriggling insects, there was none who was aware [of this], yet they were filled with a sense of alarm and fear.
Thereupon, he again placed all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions within a vessel only one foot square and round on the inside, without any crowding or compression.
The manifested transformations having reached their ultimate conclusion, they were as radiant and constant as ever.
Those seated there all witnessed this; they were all struck with wonder and leaped for joy, giving rise to great vows, their minds all abiding in the state of the Unsurpassed and Solely Honored One.
Eight million wise ones (*vidyādhara*) and various honored devas attained the samādhi of the wisdom of peace and bliss.
Furthermore, six hundred thousand people all entered the dharma-gate of penetrating understanding.
Additionally, sixty-eight thousand people attained this samādhi of the perfected and complete radiance.
All the enlightened masters who had come from the ten directions were filled with joy.
The Buddha said to Shanming:
"The reason all people do not study this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance is that they abide in delusion."

To reckon existence as existing leads one to become attached and defiled by the dark gloom; because of this attachment, it is like walking with eyes closed in the dead of night, where nothing can be seen.
That which cannot be seen refers to the good and evil of the body currently received—the very things being created before one's eyes.

"Because they see through a lack of awakening, they sigh and weep, saying: 'Now, having done good, I have instead received evil retribution; or, having previously done evil, I have instead received the blessings of goodness.'"

Failing to understand this fundamental principle, one becomes entangled in the net of doubt. Once caught in the net of doubt, one has no desire to learn what should be learned, no desire to advance where one should advance, and no desire to enter where one should enter. Consequently, one loses this meditative concentration and remains in a state of weeping, sorrow, terror, and longing. Thus, for kalpas without end, one wanders back and forth without rest; this is called the practice of toil and suffering.
"Alas, Shanming!

Because this chapter can serve as a model, the Buddha appeared in the world precisely for the sake of those who are deluded. Should there be anyone who studies this Right Concentration, whatever afflictions of birth and death they harbor will all be swiftly eliminated."
Furthermore, you are able to instruct and guide all those who are attached to existence.
Shanming! You should constantly contemplate the dharma of emptiness; do not dwell in places of delusion and error.
Subhapati addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is a worthy man born into a noble family who governs as a local official and directs the affairs of state, yet whose mind is greatly distracted and unable to remain focused, and who wishes to study this samādhi—what should he do?"
The Buddha said:

"Virtuous one, if you have the karmic conditions of serving in government office, or if you dwell in an insecure place and wish to study this samādhi but cannot focus your mind, you should write out this sūtra scroll and make offerings to it."

One should arrange seats on the pavilion, burn incense, and pay respectful homage; doing so at dawn, midday, and dusk, one does not fail the three periods of the day, prostrating with the head and face in a manner of sincere and profound devotion.
Furthermore, one should practice fifteen additional matters:
first, not killing.
Second, sustaining living beings;
third, not grasping falsely;
fourth, bestowing grace upon others.
Fifth, to refrain from sexual misconduct;
sixth, to distance oneself from forms and sounds;
seventh, to be neither deceitful nor unruly.
Eighth, to offer loyal words and provide virtuous admonition;
ninth, not to become intoxicated;
tenth, not to give alcohol as a gift.
Eleventh, to protect the weak and the lowly so as not to allow them to suffer injustice;
twelfth, to exercise benevolence toward all beings with whom one encounters in life, ensuring each finds their proper place;
thirteenth, to be broad-minded and magnanimous in receiving others, embracing even the unworthy and instructing them with the correct teaching.

Fourteenth, when those who come to seek refuge with him have grievances to present, he invariably adjudicates them with impartiality according to the law, ensuring that no one suffers injustice or resentment;
fifteenth, he encourages his superiors toward goodness and bestows its benefits upon all the people, remaining untiring from beginning to end.
Practice these fifteen precepts without ceasing or neglecting them; this is also a teaching for stabilizing the mind, which one must certainly attain without loss, leading to long-term liberation.
Subhapati addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are ordinary people who, being dragged by their past karma, dwell in a state of insecurity and are constrained and obstructed, yet possess the aspiration for this Samādhi of the Fully Perfected Radiance but cannot follow their own intentions—desiring to study this sublime concentration, what should they do?”
The Buddha said,
“Śubhaprabha! For any person who desires to study with a sincere heart, it is also as explained above.”

One should skillfully transcribe this sutra scroll, prepare a seat and canopy for it, burn incense and pay reverent homage, doing so at the three times of day without fail; furthermore, one should practice ten additional matters:
first, to cultivate and uphold the five precepts without any deficiency or transgression;
second, when at leisure, to gradually recite and practice the texts of the dhyāna-concentration teachings.
Third, although engaged in administrative duties, one should recite and practice internally so as not to forget or err;
fourth, when in a place of diligent toil and hardship, one should recognize it as the result of past karma and remain free from resentment or anger;

fifth, if one dwells in a place where there is no image of the Buddha and no assembly of the virtuous, one should always maintain mindfulness and pay homage toward the four directions as if facing the Buddha himself, without any difference.
Sixth, being cautious, admonishing oneself, and gentle, one harmonizes the mind and spirit, remaining humble toward all;
seventh, in whatever one does, one exhausts one's devotion without empty pretension;
eighth, one abounds in companionship and does not begrudge one’s own strength and labor.
Ninth, if one sees those who are aged, infirm, diseased, emaciated, or decrepit, one feels compassion and seeks to support and protect them, with a sincere heart free from artifice;
tenth, one constantly takes refuge in the Triple Gem without negligence or forgetfulness.
These are the ten matters.

Even though ordinary people may dwell in places of toil, hardship, and confinement, they should practice these ten matters; do not disparage them, and do not be indolent. Furthermore, one should fix the mind upon the teachings so that they are not lost from life to life, leading to ultimate liberation hereafter.
Subhapati said to the Buddha:
"If there is a virtuous woman from a noble family who,
due to the circumstances of her household duties and affairs, is unable to leave them behind, yet wishes to study this Samādhi of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance, what should she do?"
The Buddha said: "Śubhaprabhā!
If there are women who have domestic responsibilities and yet desire to study this right concentration, it shall be as explained above."

One should skillfully copy this sutra, set up a raised platform for it, offer and present banners and flowers, burn incense, pay homage with one's head touching the ground, and perform these acts at the three times—cockcrow, midday, and midnight—never failing in devotion. With a sincere and earnest heart, one should constantly vow to be free from the female body and sever all desire and lust, remaining thus without indolence.
Furthermore, one should apply oneself to twenty matters:
first, to uphold the fifteen precepts of the superior noble person and the ten precepts of the middling noble person without violating or defiling them;
second, to abandon the mind of envy.
Third, she diminishes her fondness for rings and bracelets;
fourth, she removes the adornment of cosmetics and rouge;
fifth, she is free from wanton gestures.
Sixth, their clothing shall be simple and pure rather than extravagant or ornate;
seventh, they shall raise those within the household with mutual kindness and compassion;
eighth, they shall instruct their servants and slaves gently, without inflicting physical pain or suffering.
Ninth, to care for the orphaned and solitary, providing them with food and clothing equitably;
tenth, to serve those above with filial piety and treat those below and small with benevolence;
eleventh, to lower one’s voice and humble one’s mind, and to practice self-reproach.
Twelfth, one should be humble and admonish oneself to be compliant, always maintaining a sense of shame and remorse;

thirteenth, whatever task one undertakes, one should handle it with hands that are pure and clean, offering it to one's elders and parents, making offerings to the Triple Gem, and providing for teachers and friends;
fourteenth, regarding those who are near or distant, and those who are good or evil, one should treat them all with equal compassion, without these four notions of discrimination.
Fifteenth, even when in a private chamber, empty and secluded with no one present, his mind does not harbor thoughts of desire;
sixteenth, he is upright, earnest, and single-minded, his mind always abiding in the Dharma;
seventeenth, whatever he intends to undertake, he first reports it to those he honors, and only then proceeds to act.
Eighteenth, one should have no mind of self-will, but always admonish oneself with humility and obedience so that one acts in accordance with the True Dharma;
nineteenth, one must never peer through walls or enclosures with depraved thoughts;
twentieth, in sitting, rising, or speaking, one must never engage in frivolous jesting, but always remain in accord with the law and precepts without negligence or transgression.
"This is the method for a virtuous woman to practice right concentration while living at home.
By not allowing this to leak away, her merit will gradually be fulfilled, and she will ultimately attain long-term liberation.
Subhā addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there be women of humble birth and common station who by nature delight in practicing the conduct of the worthy, yet whose families are poor and beset by calamity, who endure the toil of menial labor, who are burdened with anxiety over food and clothing and lack self-mastery, and who inwardly loathe their misfortunes and sins, desiring swift liberation—if such as these hear of this pure dharma of the Samādhi of the Honored One of Perfect Radiance and wish to practice it with a sincere heart, what should they do?"
The Buddha said, “Śubhavimalā!

As for ordinary women like these who live in poverty and wish to study this samādhi, even if they cannot fully practice the precepts, they should nevertheless cultivate and uphold ten matters and must not violate or abandon them.”
First, one personally approaches a virtuous friend to receive the five precepts and practices them without violation or deficiency;
second, though hungry or cold, one endures not killing or stealing so as to satisfy oneself with warmth;
third, though dwelling alone, one endures not sexual misconduct and frequently admonishes the mind.
Fourth, though poor, one endures not to deceive or be indolent in order to seek wealth;
fifth, regarding wine, food, and performers, one endures not to watch such spectacles;
sixth, one honors those who practice the Dharma of concentration, regarding them as Buddhas.
Seventh, one should constantly practice five virtuous states of mind:

first, the mind of mindfulness toward giving; second, the mind of reverence; third, the mind of propriety; fourth, the mind of being humble toward all; and fifth, the mind of subduing various worldly dispositions.
Eighth, even while engaged in worldly affairs, one should recite the Dharma texts in the mind without indolence.
Ninth, on the six fast days, one enters the stupa to pay homage to the Three Honored Ones;

tenth, although one may have no wealth to offer as alms, one should always personally sweep and sprinkle the stupa grounds with pure water, providing it for the monastic community to wash their hands and bathe, performing acts of giving according to one's strength, diligent and without weariness.

This is what it means for an ordinary woman in poverty to practice these ten matters without indolence; this is truly sublime. She shall be born to encounter a Buddha, constantly meet with the fixed Dharma, and ultimately attain long-term liberation.
The Buddha said: “Shanming!

Regarding what I have taught concerning the virtuous woman, the ordinary woman, the noble-born virtuous woman, and the ordinary-born woman who practices good conduct—these four categories of conduct are clearly defined by the admonitory Dharma.
